The Sahara was once grassland
slides.body: Rainy spells lasting many thousands of years brought more lakes and rivers. The Sahara became savanna.

slides.headline: Dry spells scatter wildlife
slides.body: Lakes fall and rivers dry up. Plants and animals retreat north, south or east, splitting groups apart. That may give rise to new species.

slides.headline: Even human journeys follow the pump
slides.body: Scientists have used the Saharan pump to date waves of human migration from Africa, from Homo erectus to Homo sapiens.

slides.headline: The Sahara works like a pump.
slides.body: It moved plants and animals, and has been used to date human migrations.

caption:
The Sahara was once grassland. It keeps flipping.

Long, rainy spells have turned the Sahara and Arabia into savanna grassland, with more lakes and rivers. African plants and animals became common there. The last green phase began about 12,500 BC and peaked around 4000 BC.

The catch? The green never lasts. When the rains retreat, lakes fall and rivers dry up. Plants and animals retreat north, south or east, and groups get split apart. That may give rise to new species.

The payoff? This is the Sahara pump theory. It explains how plants and animals moved between Africa and Eurasia, and it has been used to date waves of human migration from Africa.
